questions.prompt: A length is measured as (2.40 ± 0.05) m. (a) Calculate the percentage uncertainty. (2) (b) The length is squared to obtain an area proportional to $L^2$. Estimate the percentage uncertainty in the area. (2) (c) Explain the difference between a random and a systematic error. (3)
hints: For powers, multiply fractional uncertainty by the power.
questions.solution: (a) Percentage uncertainty $=0.05/2.40\times100=2.08\%$. (b) For $L^2$, percentage uncertainty $\approx2\times2.08=4.17\%$. (c) Random errors vary unpredictably between readings and can be reduced by repeats; systematic errors shift readings consistently and are not removed by averaging. [M1 A1 B1 M1 A1 B1 M1]

questions.solution: (a) Percentage uncertainty $=0.05/2.40\times100=2.08\%$. (b) For $L^2$, percentage uncertainty $\approx2\times2.08=4.17\%$. (c) Random errors vary unpredictably between readings and can be reduced by repeats; systematic errors shift readings consistently and are not removed by averaging. [M1 A1 B1 M1 A1 B1 M1]

questions.prompt: A radioactive isotope has half-life 3.0 h. (a) Calculate the fraction of an initial sample remaining after 9 h. (2) (b) Explain why radioactive decay is described as random but follows an exponential law for a large sample. (3) (c) State one safety precaution when handling a sealed source. (1)
hints: Distinguish individual unpredictability from population behaviour.
questions.solution: (a) Number of half-lives $=3$, so fraction remaining $=(1/2)^{3}=0.1250$. (b) The decay time of an individual nucleus cannot be predicted, but each nucleus has a constant probability of decay per unit time, giving an exponential decrease for many nuclei. (c) e.g. use tongs, shielding, minimise exposure time, maximise distance. [M1 A1 B1 M1 A1 B1]

questions.solution: (a) $\lambda=c/f=6.667e-07$ m. (b) $E=hf=2.983e-19$ J. (c) Diffraction is spreading of waves at an aperture/edge and is greatest when the aperture size is comparable with the wavelength. [M1 A1 B1 M1 A1 B1 M1]

questions.prompt: A body of mass 2.0 kg is pulled horizontally by a force of 12 N. A resistive force of 3 N acts in the opposite direction. (a) Calculate the acceleration. (3) (b) Starting from rest, calculate the speed after 4.0 s assuming constant acceleration. (2) (c) Explain one limitation of the constant-resistance model. (2)
questions.solution: (a) Resultant force $=12-3=9$ N. $a=F/m=4.50$ m s$^{-2}$. (b) $v=u+at=0+4.50\times4=18.00$ m s$^{-1}$. (c) Real drag generally changes with speed/environment, so it is unlikely to remain constant. [M1 A1 B1 M1 A1 B1 M1]

questions.solution: (a) Resultant force $=12-3=9$ N. $a=F/m=4.50$ m s$^{-2}$. (b) $v=u+at=0+4.50\times4=18.00$ m s$^{-1}$. (c) Real drag generally changes with speed/environment, so it is unlikely to remain constant. [M1 A1 B1 M1 A1 B1 M1]

questions.prompt: Two resistors, 100 $\Omega$ and 200 $\Omega$, are connected in series to an ideal 6 V supply. (a) Calculate the current. questions.prompt: A spherical body has mass $5.97e+24$ kg and radius $6.37e+06$ m. (a) Calculate the gravitational field strength at its surface. Use $G=6.67\times10^{-11}$ N m$^2$ kg$^{-2}$. (3) (b) State how field strength changes with distance outside the body. (2) (c) Explain why gravitational potential is negative when zero is defined at infinity. (2)
hints: Potential is defined relative to infinity.
questions.solution: (a) $g=GM/r^2=9.81$ N kg$^{-1}$. (b) Outside a spherical body $g\propto1/r^2$. (c) Work must be supplied to move a mass from the field to infinity, so bound positions have lower (negative) potential relative to the zero at infinity. [M1 A1 B1 M1 A1 B1 M1]

(3) (b) State how field strength changes with distance outside the body. (2) (c) Explain why gravitational potential is negative when zero is defined at infinity. (2)
hints: Potential is defined relative to infinity.
questions.solution: (a) $g=GM/r^2=1.62$ N kg$^{-1}$. (b) Outside a spherical body $g\propto1/r^2$. (c) Work must be supplied to move a mass from the field to infinity, so bound positions have lower (negative) potential relative to the zero at infinity. [M1 A1 B1 M1 A1 B1 M1]

questions.prompt: A radioactive isotope has half-life 3.0 h. (a) Calculate the fraction of an initial sample remaining after 9 h. (2) (b) Explain why radioactive decay is described as random but follows an exponential law for a large sample. (3) (c) State one safety precaution when handling a sealed source. (1)
hints: Distinguish individual unpredictability from population behaviour.
questions.solution: (a) Number of half-lives $=3$, so fraction remaining $=(1/2)^{3}=0.1250$. (b) The decay time of an individual nucleus cannot be predicted, but each nucleus has a constant probability of decay per unit time, giving an exponential decrease for many nuclei. (c) e.g. use tongs, shielding, minimise exposure time, maximise distance. [M1 A1 B1 M1 A1 B1]

questions.prompt: A radioactive isotope has half-life 5.0 h. (a) Calculate the fraction of an initial sample remaining after 15 h. (2) (b) Explain why radioactive decay is described as random but follows an exponential law for a large sample. (3) (c) State one safety precaution when handling a sealed source. (1)
hints: Distinguish individual unpredictability from population behaviour.
questions.solution: (a) Number of half-lives $=3$, so fraction remaining $=(1/2)^{3}=0.1250$. (b) The decay time of an individual nucleus cannot be predicted, but each nucleus has a constant probability of decay per unit time, giving an exponential decrease for many nuclei. (c) e.g. use tongs, shielding, minimise exposure time, maximise distance. [M1 A1 B1 M1 A1 B1]

questions.solution: (a) Percentage uncertainty $=0.10/4.80\times100=2.08\%$. (b) For $L^2$, percentage uncertainty $\approx2\times2.08=4.17\%$. (c) Random errors vary unpredictably between readings and can be reduced by repeats; systematic errors shift readings consistently and are not removed by averaging. [M1 A1 B1 M1 A1 B1 M1]

questions.prompt: An ideal gas is at temperature 300 K. (a) Calculate the mean translational kinetic energy per molecule using $\frac32kT$. (2) (b) Explain microscopically why gas pressure increases when temperature rises at constant volume. (3) (c) State one assumption of the ideal-gas model. (1)
hints: Pressure comes from momentum changes at the walls.
questions.solution: (a) $E=\frac32kT=6.210e-21$ J. (b) Molecules have greater mean speed, collide with the walls more frequently and with greater momentum change, increasing force per unit area. questions.solution: (a) $E=\frac32kT=9.315e-21$ J. (b) Molecules have greater mean speed, collide with the walls more frequently and with greater momentum change, increasing force per unit area. (c) e.g. negligible molecular volume or no intermolecular forces except during collisions. [M1 A1 B1 M1 A1 B1]

questions.prompt: A radioactive isotope has half-life 3.0 h. (a) Calculate the fraction of an initial sample remaining after 9 h. (2) (b) Explain why radioactive decay is described as random but follows an exponential law for a large sample. (3) (c) State one safety precaution when handling a sealed source. (1)
hints: Distinguish individual unpredictability from population behaviour.
questions.solution: (a) Number of half-lives $=3$, so fraction remaining $=(1/2)^{3}=0.1250$. (b) The decay time of an individual nucleus cannot be predicted, but each nucleus has a constant probability of decay per unit time, giving an exponential decrease for many nuclei. (c) e.g. use tongs, shielding, minimise exposure time, maximise distance. [M1 A1 B1 M1 A1 B1]

questions.prompt: A student plots a graph to test a proposed linear relationship between two physical quantities. (a) Explain how the gradient can be used to determine a physical constant. (2) (b) Describe two ways to reduce uncertainty in the gradient. (2) (c) Explain why a straight-line graph alone does not prove the proposed model is exact. (2)
hints: A large gradient triangle reduces percentage reading uncertainty.
questions.solution: (a) Rearrange the model into $y=mx+c$ and identify the constant from the theoretical expression for $m$. (b) Use a wide range of values and a best-fit line/large triangle; repeat measurements where appropriate. (c) Experimental uncertainty and a limited data range may hide small systematic deviations from the model. [M1 A1 B1 M1 A1 B1]

hints: A large gradient triangle reduces percentage reading uncertainty.
questions.solution: (a) Rearrange the model into $y=mx+c$ and identify the constant from the theoretical expression for $m$. (b) Use a wide range of values and a best-fit line/large triangle; repeat measurements where appropriate. (c) Experimental uncertainty and a limited data range may hide small systematic deviations from the model. [M1 A1 B1 M1 A1 B1]

hints: A large gradient triangle reduces percentage reading uncertainty.
questions.solution: (a) Rearrange the model into $y=mx+c$ and identify the constant from the theoretical expression for $m$. (b) Use a wide range of values and a best-fit line/large triangle; repeat measurements where appropriate. (c) Experimental uncertainty and a limited data range may hide small systematic deviations from the model. [M1 A1 B1 M1 A1 B1]

questions.prompt: Two resistors, 100 $\Omega$ and 200 $\Omega$, are connected in series to an ideal 6 V supply. (a) Calculate the current. questions.solution: (a) $R_T=300\,\Omega$, so $I=V/R=0.0200$ A. (b) $V_2=IR_2=4.00$ V. (c) Parallel connection gives a smaller total resistance than either branch, so for the same supply voltage the total current is larger. [M1 A1 B1 M1 A1 B1]
